subject: physics_2
question_text: A steel wire 0.72m long has a mass of 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg. If the wire is under a tension of 60N, what is the speed of transverse waves on the wire?

verification.note: The 1+2+2+2+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. It needs that teacher pass more than most cards on this paper: an 8-mark split for a SHORT numerical is not a thing any printed scheme shows, because the book files this numerical under Long Answer numbering with no Problems banner, so the 8 marks come from the section it sits in and the five-way split across them is entirely this bank's invention. A teacher may well mark it as a 4-mark question. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Arithmetic hand-checked: μ = m/l = 5.0 × 10⁻³ / 0.72 = 6.944 × 10⁻³ ≈ 6.9 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹; v = √(T/μ) = √(60 / 6.9 × 10⁻³) = √8696 = 93.25 ≈ 93 m s⁻¹ — agrees with the book's printed 93 m s⁻¹ (carrying μ unrounded gives √8640 = 92.95, which rounds to the same 93). The book's question text prints "transvere waves"; the misspelling is corrected to "transverse" here, and the wording is otherwise preserved.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order — the data, the linear density, the speed formula, the substitution, and the result.

steps.label: Data listed
lines: Transverse waves on a stretched wire.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Three data lines, all in SI units already.
steps.why: Every quantity here is already in SI units, so the only place an error can enter is the powers of ten in the mass — writing them on their own line keeps them visible.
common_mistakes: Reading 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg as the linear density. It is the mass of the whole wire.
Using the tension as a mass. T = 60 N is a force.

recall.must_convey: That l = 0.72 m, m = 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg and T = 60 N.
accept: length zero point seven two metre

steps.memory_tip: Three numbers, three lines — length, mass, tension, in that order.

steps.label: Linear density
lines: Linear density is the mass per unit
steps.margin_note: Two marks: the definition μ = m/l, then its value with the unit kg m⁻¹.
steps.why: The speed formula needs mass per metre, not the mass of the wire, so this division is a separate step and carries its own marks.
common_mistakes: Putting the total mass straight into √(T/μ). The wire is 0.72 m long, so divide first.
Dropping the unit kg m⁻¹, which is what shows μ is a density and not a mass.

accept: linear density is mass per unit length
reject: square root of T by mu

steps.memory_tip: Mass of the wire divided by its length — a per-metre number, so the unit is kg m⁻¹.

steps.label: Wave speed formula
lines: The speed of a transverse wave on a
stretched wire depends on the tension

steps.margin_note: Two marks for the formula alone. Write it before any number goes in.
steps.why: v = √(T/μ) is a standard result and may be quoted here without deriving it; the marks are for the correct placing of T and μ.
common_mistakes: Writing v = √(μ/T). A tighter wire carries faster waves, so T belongs on top.
Forgetting the square root and reporting T/μ as the speed.

recall.must_convey: That the speed of a transverse wave on a stretched wire is v = √(T/μ).
accept: v is root T by mu
square root of tension by linear density

steps.memory_tip: Tighter wire, faster wave — so tension goes on top of the fraction.

steps.label: Substitution
lines: Substituting the tension and the linear
steps.margin_note: Two marks: one substitution line, then the value under the root.
steps.why: Reducing the fraction to 8.70 × 10³ before taking the root keeps the powers of ten in one place, which is where this numerical is usually lost.
common_mistakes: Dividing 60 by 6.9 and forgetting the 10⁻³, which gives 8.7 instead of 8700.
Trying to root 8.70 and 10³ separately. The power of ten is odd, so write 8.70 × 10³ as 8700 before taking the root.

accept: 60 divided by 6 point 9 into 10 power minus 3
eight point seven into ten cube

steps.memory_tip: Dividing by 10⁻³ multiplies by 1000 — the number under the root jumps to about 8700.

steps.label: Result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Give the answer with the unit m s⁻¹.
steps.why: 90² is 8100 and 95² is 9025, so the root of 8700 has to sit between them — a check that takes a moment and catches a misplaced power of ten.
common_mistakes: Writing 93 with no unit. Speed is in metres per second.

recall.must_convey: That the square root of about 8700 is about 93 m s⁻¹.

steps.memory_tip: 90² = 8100 and 95² = 9025, so √8700 has to land near 93.

insider_note: Two divisions decide this numerical: mass by length to reach μ, then tension by μ under the root. A student who skips the first one puts the whole 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg into the formula and reports about 110 m s⁻¹ instead of 93 m s⁻¹.
